summary: This informational document describes privacy issues of using the DNS and gives general observations about typical current privacy practices. It is an analysis of the present situation and does not prescribe solutions. It obsoletes RFC 7626.

plainLanguage.summary: A DNS lookup can reveal the names a device is trying to reach. RFC 9076 describes who may see those queries and what patterns can reveal, without setting requirements or defining solutions.

subtitle: An analysis of what DNS queries reveal and which parties can observe them.

tldr.problem: DNS queries reveal which names a user looks up to recursive resolvers and, in some cases, authoritative name servers or network observers.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes privacy risks in DNS data, network transports, recursive resolvers, authoritative servers, and inferences from query patterns. It describes the situation and does not prescribe solutions.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9076 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 7626. Its recommendations are outside scope; it points to other documents for operator guidance.

today: RFC 9076 is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 7626. It analyzes DNS privacy practices and does not prescribe solutions.

sections.title: How a DNS Lookup Reaches Servers
sections.content:
A stub resolver on a device sends a query to a recursive resolver. If the answer is not cached, that resolver asks authoritative name servers, such as root and top-level-domain servers, for information.

In the example in the RFC, each authoritative server receives the original full question unless the resolver uses QNAME minimization. The recursive resolver typically sees all queries from the device, while caching means authoritative servers see only some of them.
sections.plainLanguage: Your device sends a DNS question to a resolver, which may ask other servers for the answer. Those servers can receive the name you asked about.

sections.title: The Analysis Focuses on the End User
sections.content:
The RFC focuses on privacy risks to the person making DNS requests, including risks from broad or targeted monitoring. It describes typical practices rather than comparing the protections of individual networks or organizations.

Privacy risks to zone holders, risks to resolver operators such as leakage of private namespaces, and non-privacy issues such as cache poisoning are outside the document's scope. It also does not analyze every device and network context for one user.
sections.plainLanguage: This document examines what DNS activity can reveal about the person making requests. It leaves several other DNS and security questions outside its scope.

sections.title: What DNS Data Can Reveal
sections.content:
A DNS query includes the QNAME, the name being looked up, and the source address. The QNAME can reveal the service or domain a user is contacting; a sequence of queries can reveal patterns of activity. The source address usually identifies the user's device between the stub and recursive resolver.

Between a recursive resolver and an authoritative server, the source is usually the resolver's address. The EDNS Client Subnet option can pass client address information onward. The RFC also describes cache snooping as a way to infer what names other clients have queried.
sections.plainLanguage: The requested name can reveal what service a person is trying to reach. A series of requests can reveal more than any one request by itself.

sections.title: Risks on the Network Path
sections.content:
Unencrypted DNS can be read by an observer on the network path. DNSSEC does not provide confidentiality. Encrypted transports such as DNS over TLS and DNS over HTTPS hide the DNS payload from passive observers on that connection.

Encryption does not remove every privacy risk. The RFC describes how message size and timing, client fingerprints, connection reuse, or HTTP headers can help correlate queries or identify clients.
sections.plainLanguage: Encryption hides the words in a DNS query from passive observers on that connection. Timing, message size, and other connection details can still reveal patterns.

sections.title: Recursive and Authoritative Resolver Risks
sections.content:
Recursive resolvers see most of a device's DNS traffic, so the resolver choice has privacy consequences. Many users keep the resolver supplied by their network, while some use public resolvers. Operators may keep query logs or share data with others.

Authoritative servers see fewer queries because of caching and QNAME minimization, but they still see some traffic. A local resolver may expose the end user's source address to them, and EDNS Client Subnet can pass address information through a shared resolver.
sections.plainLanguage: The recursive resolver is in a position to see many of a device's DNS questions. Authoritative servers see fewer questions, but may still receive identifying address information.

sections.title: Inference and the Limits of This RFC
sections.content:
The RFC describes how observers can infer identity from query patterns and cites a study reporting 73.1% correct day-to-day links. It also discusses surveillance and the use of DNS data to analyze activity.

The document is an analysis of privacy risks, not a specification of solutions or requirements. It obsoletes RFC 7626 and points to RFC 8932 for recommendations to DNS privacy service operators.
sections.plainLanguage: Patterns across DNS queries can help an observer recognize a user. This RFC describes the risks but does not require a particular fix.
